claims.text: The as-manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy has a mainly single-phase FCC matrix.
The as-manufactured alloy contains residual porosity and heterogeneous or high-energy grain boundaries.
The as-manufactured alloy has minimal native oxide content.
Elevated-temperature degradation is primarily governed by selective oxidation of Ti and Al at manufacturing-induced defect sites.
TiO2 and Al2O3 are expected oxidation products in the target alloy.
Residual pores and grain boundaries promote rapid oxygen diffusion and preferential oxide formation.
Non-uniform oxide growth produces local stress concentrations.
Thermal-expansion mismatch between oxide scales and the substrate generates local tensile stresses that cause scale spallation.
Scale spallation exposes fresh metal and accelerates further oxidation.
The oxidation and spallation cycle accelerates crack initiation and propagation and can cause catastrophic failure under mechanical load.
Changing oxygen partial pressure between oxidizing and reducing atmospheres will alter oxidation behavior.
Oxidizing exposure will produce thicker, more inhomogeneous oxide layers concentrated at defect sites.
Oxidizing exposure will reduce ductility and cause premature mechanical failure relative to the starting-state baseline.
Reducing exposure will significantly suppress oxide formation.
Reducing exposure will delay degradation and improve retention of mechanical properties.
The proposed mechanism applies between 700 and 900 °C when oxygen partial pressure is high enough to promote rapid oxidation.
Lowering oxygen partial pressure outside the oxidizing boundary will slow degradation.
Similar oxide scales and failure modes under oxidizing and reducing conditions would falsify the proposed governing mechanism.
